newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Koebnick says timely EMU paramount.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Koebnick says timely EMU paramount.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said on Wednesday it would be better to allow Germany some leeway in meeting the criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) than to delay launching the project.

Departing from a stance he shared with other Bundesbank officials that strict adherence outweighed the timetable, Koebnick said he favoured a punctual start to EMU on January 1, 1999 even if it emerged that Germany "would not be a good fulfiller of the criteria."
Koebnick said it now made little sense to consider a delay as Bonn's budget position was unlikely to improve in the coming two years.

"I cannot see at present how Germany can meet the deficit criterion without tricks in 1999," Koebnick, who is also president of the state central bank for Rhineland Palatinate and the Saarland, told a news conference.
Raising petrol tax and cutting spending were measures with which the deficit problem could be tackled, he said.
Koebnick said Bonn would be seen as opting out of monetary union if it caused a delay by exceeding the deficit target.

It would be "more than embarrassing" if Germany missed the key deficit criterion. Bonn's voice would lose weight if it had to depend on countries with a lesser tradition of stability to approve its membership of the single currency, Koebnick said.
But estimates showed tax revenues in 1998 and 1999 were likely to be even worse than in 1997, the key year for deciding which nations can join EMU, Koebnick said.

While Bonn plans to cut the deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 -- just below the three percent ceiling set by the Maastricht Treaty -- independent economists expect it to overshoot that target as persistently high unemployment squeezes revenues.
The treaty gives countries leeway to exceed the limit in certain circumstances.

"If we cause a postponement or even a failure of EMU due to an overshoot of the deficit limit, many of our partners would see this as the German variant of the opt-out clause," Koebnick told a news conference.

Koebnick said Bonn's plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves was unfortunately timed because it coincided with news of a tax revenue shortfall which had intensified the debate about whether Germany could qualify.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, faced with news of an 18 billion-mark shortfall in 1997 tax revenues, last Thursday announced plans to value the Bundesbank's reserves closer to market levels in a bid to reduce public debt.

The plan has been attacked as a desperate piece of creative accounting designed to ensure Germany meets the fiscal convergence criteria for deficit and debt of no more than three percent and 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) respectively.
Koebnick on Wednesday declined to comment on the revaluation, saying he wanted to wait for the government to present draft proposals of the plan to the Bundesbank's policy-making council.

But he said: "It was not a happy coincidence that it was announced in this period and I think that lawmakers must look carefully at the Federal Republic's and the Bundesbank's position in the process towards EMU."
Koebnick said the best solution for EMU would be a punctual start with six to eight members whose currencies had a proven track record of stability.

Referring to the chances of Italy, Spain and Portugal to be among the starting members, Koebnick said concentrating on the need for sustainability of the criteria may lead to a differentiation between how those countries are judged.
"It could be sensible that the three do not all join at the same time, but all are likely to be in monetary union by 2002."
